transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. Please don't check anything inside the casing. Put the cover back on and screw it down before you plug it in again. I know the YouTube videos make it look routine, but the high-voltage capacitor in a microwave can hold a lethal charge even after it's been unplugged for a while. Testing the magnetron, diode or capacitor is a job for a qualified engineer, not a DIY one. The light, turntable and fan all work but the food stays cold. That usually means the low-voltage side is fine and the problem is in the high-voltage heating circuit. The faulty part could be the magnetron, but it could equally be the HV diode, the HV capacitor or, on inverter models, the inverter board. Only an engineer's test can tell which. Before you go down that route, rule out the simple causes, all from the outside: 1. Check the setting. Make sure it isn't on defrost, a low power level, or a grill or combination mode, and that a timed cook has actually started (not just the clock being set). If it was on a low power or another mode, set it to full power and try again. That may be the whole problem.
2. Do a water test. Put a microwave-safe mug of water in on full power for one minute. If the water is hot, it's heating and the issue is the setting or the cookware. If it's still cold, that suggests a heating-circuit fault.
3. Check the door. It should click firmly shut, with no food or debris on the latch hooks or the frame. A door that isn't fully latching can stop it heating even when other parts run. If the water still comes out cold on full power with the door latching properly, it needs an engineer. Do also listen for an unusually loud or heavy buzz while it runs, as that's useful to tell them. On a cheaper microwave the repair can cost close to the price of a new one, so get a quote before you commit. Whichever way it goes, stop using it if you smell burning or see smoke. Did the water test, 1 minute on full power and the water stayed cold. Door closes fine and it's the same on every power level. The hum is quieter than it used to be, and there was one loud buzz just before it stopped heating. It's unplugged now though, so what's the likely culprit?

With the water staying cold on full power, the door latching properly and every power level behaving the same, the setting and the door are effectively ruled out. That leaves a fault in the high-voltage heating circuit. The loud buzz just before it stopped heating, followed by a quieter hum since, fits a part in that circuit failing suddenly. A quieter hum often means the transformer is no longer working hard because nothing downstream is drawing power. On a conventional (transformer) microwave, the order of suspicion would be: 1. The magnetron. It's the most common cause of 'runs but no heat', especially after a bang or buzz.
2. The HV diode. It can short with a heavy buzz and then fail open, which can blow the internal fuse or stop heating.
3. The HV capacitor. This is less likely, but it often fails at the same time as the diode. Some Samsung models are inverter types instead. On those, there is no transformer, diode or capacitor, and the inverter board becomes the main suspect alongside the magnetron. I'm fairly confident it's this circuit, but which part has failed can only be confirmed by an engineer testing it safely, so I wouldn't buy anything yet. In the meantime, please put the cover screws back in and don't run it again. Repeated use with a failed HV part can damage the others. The model number will tell us whether it's conventional or inverter. That narrows the likely part and helps you get an accurate quote. As a rough guide, a magnetron plus labour on a basic solo microwave often costs close to the price of a new one. On a higher-end combi or built-in model, repair is usually worth it. Could you read me the model number from the rating plate? It's usually inside the door frame or on the back. Is it badged 'inverter' anywhere?
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.
Model number is MS23K3513AW/EU. Doesn't say inverter anywhere that I've seen. Cost about £100 new so I'm probably just going to bin it or fix it myself, but which part is it likely to be?

Since it isn't badged inverter anywhere, it's most likely a conventional transformer type. 1. Magnetron. This is the most likely part. 2. HV diode. This is a close second. Diodes often short with a heavy buzz and then stop the heating altogether.
3. HV capacitor. This is less likely on its own, but it sometimes fails together with the diode. I'd put it at roughly evens to better that it's the magnetron. The buzz pattern genuinely fits the diode too, though, and only a proper high-voltage test tells them apart. On fixing it yourself: please don't. Every one of those parts sits in the high-voltage section, and the capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when unplugged. It isn't a case of being careful enough. It's simply not a safe DIY job. Please put the cover screws back in whatever you decide. On a £100 solo microwave, replacing it is the sensible call. A magnetron plus an engineer's labour will usually cost about the same as a new one, or more. Even a cheaper diode repair still means paying for a call-out and a test. If you replace it, take the old one to your local household recycling centre's small electricals (WEEE) bin rather than putting it in general waste. Some retailers will also take it back when they deliver a new one.
